title: How to patch a small hole in drywall in an afternoon
excerpt: A doorknob hole looks bad but takes less than an hour of real work. Here's how we do it, and when it's worth calling us.
content:
Most drywall holes we see come from door handles, picture hooks and moving furniture. Anything smaller than a fist is a job you can do yourself.

Clean up the edges

Cut away loose paper and crumbs with a sharp utility knife, so the patch has something solid to stick to.

Use a self-adhesive patch

For holes up to four inches, a mesh patch from the hardware store is the easiest fix. Press it flat over the hole.

Three thin coats, not one thick one

Spread joint compound over the patch with a wide knife, feathering it out past the edges. Let it dry, sand lightly and repeat twice.

Match the texture

Most Orlando walls have an orange peel texture. A can of spray texture makes the patch disappear before you paint.

When to call us

Holes bigger than a hand, water-stained ceilings and cracks that keep coming back need more than a patch. Send us a photo for a free price.

title: Five things painters do that make a room look professional
excerpt: The difference between a good paint job and a great one is mostly what happens before the roller comes out.
content:
Anyone can roll paint on a wall. What makes a room look professional is the hour of preparation first.

Fill every hole

Nail holes and dents show up badly in fresh paint. Fill them, let them dry and sand them flat.

Caulk the gaps

A thin bead of paintable caulk where trim meets the wall makes every line look crisp.

Prime the patches

Filler soaks up paint differently from the wall. A dab of primer stops the patches from showing through.

Cut in first

Brush a neat band along the ceiling and trim before rolling, and keep a wet edge so you don't get lines.

Two coats, always

One coat almost never covers evenly, even with paint and primer in one. Plan for two.

title: How to keep a wooden deck going in the Florida sun
excerpt: Sun, rain and humidity are hard on wood. A little care each spring adds years to a deck.
content:
A well-kept deck in Central Florida should last twenty years. A neglected one can rot through in eight.

Look for soft spots

Each spring, press a screwdriver into the boards, the posts and the ends of the stair treads. If it sinks in easily, the wood is rotting.

Wash it, gently

A deck cleaner and a stiff brush do more good than a pressure washer, which can tear up the grain.

Seal it every two years

A penetrating sealer with UV protection keeps water out and slows the graying. Seal on a dry, cool morning.

Keep the gaps clear

Leaves and dirt between boards hold water against the wood. Clear them out with a putty knife.

Fix small problems early

A loose rail or one soft board is a quick repair. Left for a few seasons, it can mean rebuilding the steps.

title: Why your doors stick every summer (and how to fix it)
excerpt: Florida humidity makes wooden doors swell. Here's how to tell what's going on, and the quick fixes that work.
content:
If a door closes fine in January and sticks in July, the wood is swelling with the humidity. Sometimes the fix takes five minutes.

Tighten the hinges first

Loose hinge screws let a door sag and rub at the top corner. Tighten them, or swap the top screw for a longer one that reaches the frame.

Find where it rubs

Rub chalk along the edge of the door, close it, and see where the chalk comes off. That's the spot to fix.

Seal every edge

Doors swell when bare edges soak up moisture. Paint or seal the top and bottom edges too, not just the faces.

Plane only as a last resort

If it still sticks, a little planing on the rubbing edge fixes it. Take off less than you think, and seal it afterwards.

Check the weatherstripping

While you're there, look at the seal around the door. If you can see daylight, your cool air is leaking out. We can replace it in under an hour.
